anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De Oratione exists (only copyrighted Greer/O'Meara/Oulton-Chadwick); nothing to compare against. Sense checked against the Greek and the cited Scripture wording.

apparatus: Title absent in T; kept per Pamphilus + Origen cross-ref.
egenthe vs egennethe: kept 'became' (majority + Pauline sense).
T lacuna after charizetai (~225 letters, John 15:14-15 matter): marked, supplements refused.
Post-lacuna clause illegible in scan: not rendered; intact 1 Cor 2:11-13 translated.

choices.why: hupertetes = subordinate servant/assistant; 'servant' keeps Christ's subordinate role in Origen's economy without importing later office language.
synergos is active: the Spirit works alongside; hyphenated form marks it as one title.
epikeros = death-doomed; distinguished from phtharton soma (corruptible body) in the Wisdom quote two lines later.
exichniazo = track by footprints; Paul 'tracks' heaven having been there; kept consistent across all four uses.
Origen's hedge about Paul is load-bearing (voice card: preserve hedges); tacha kept as 'perhaps'.

lemmas.lexica: LSJ adverb: quickly; as particle: perhaps

pass_a_gloss: The things, by being greatest and beyond man, turning out excessively beyond our mortal nature, impossible for the rational and mortal race to grasp — these become possible in much and unmeasured grace being poured out from God to men by God through Jesus Christ the servant of the unsurpassable-toward-us grace and the co-working Spirit, by God's will. At any rate the acquisition of Wisdom (by whom all things were constructed — for 'in wisdom God made them all' per David), being impossible for human nature, becomes possible out of impossible through our Lord Jesus Christ, who 'became wisdom to us from God, both righteousness and sanctification and redemption.' For 'what man shall know God's counsel? or who shall conceive what the Lord wills? since mortals' counsels are timid and our notions insecure; for a corruptible body weighs down soul, and an earthy tent weighs down a much-caring mind. And hardly do we conjecture earthly things; heavenly things, who has tracked out?' Who would not say tracking out heavenly things is impossible for man? But nevertheless this impossible becomes possible by God's surpassing grace; for he who was caught up to a third heaven perhaps tracked out the things in the three heavens, having heard 'unspeakable words which a man is not allowed to speak.' Who can say a man may come to know the Lord's mind? But even this God grants through Christ. [GAP] But 'as no one of men knows the things of the man except the man's spirit in him, so too no one knows God's things except God's Spirit.' If no one knows God's things except God's Spirit, knowing God's things is impossible for man. Consider how even this becomes possible: 'But we,' he says, 'received not the world's spirit but the Spirit from God, that we may know the things granted us by God, which we also speak not in taught-by-human-wisdom words but in Spirit-taught ones.'
pass_b_english: Some things are so great, so far beyond man — so far past what our mortal nature can reach — that our rational and dying race cannot possibly grasp them. Yet they become possible when God pours out his grace upon men, great grace beyond measure, through Jesus Christ, the servant of his unsurpassable grace toward us, and through the co-working Spirit — all by the will of God.

Take the possession of Wisdom, by whom all things were made — for, as David says, in wisdom God made them all. For human nature as it stands this is impossible; yet out of the impossible it becomes possible, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who became wisdom to us from God — righteousness and sanctification and redemption.

For what man shall know the counsel of God? Or who shall conceive what the Lord wills? Since the reasonings of mortals are timid, and our notions insecure. For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthy tent burdens a mind crowded with cares. Hardly do we guess at the things on earth — but the things in heaven, who has ever traced them out?

Who would deny that it is impossible for a man to trace out the things in heaven? And yet even this impossible thing becomes possible by God's surpassing grace. For the one who was caught up to the third heaven perhaps did trace out the things in the three heavens — since he had heard unspeakable words, which no man is permitted to utter.

Who could say it is possible for a man to come to know the mind of the Lord? Yet even this God grants through Christ. [Here the chief manuscript has a gap of about three and a half lines, which held a discussion of the words in John 15; the conjectural fillings proposed by editors are not rendered as Origen's text.]

But as no one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man within him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. And if no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, it is impossible for a man to know the things of God. Consider too how even this becomes possible. We, he says, received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, that we might know the things freely given us by God — things we speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit (Titus 3:5–6) (Psalm 104:24) (1 Corinthians 1:30) (Wisdom 9:13–16) (2 Corinthians 12:2) (2 Corinthians 12:4) (Romans 11:34) (1 Corinthians 2:16) (1 Corinthians 2:11) (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).
